chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: One morning Gregor Samsa woke up from bad dreams. He was in his bed, and he was not a man any more. He was a huge, horrible **insect**.

He lay on his back, and his back was very hard, like metal. When he lifted his head a little, he could see his brown **belly**. It was a little round, and lines across it divided it into hard parts. The blanket was almost falling off the bed. It could not cover his belly well. He had many legs, but they were very thin and weak for such a big body. He looked at them. They moved helplessly in the air, and he could not stop them.

"What has happened to me?" he thought. It was not a dream. His room was a real room, a human room, only a little too small. It was quiet, and the four walls were the same as always. On the table there were many cloth **samples**. Gregor was a travelling **salesman**. Above the table there was a picture. Not long before, he had cut it out of a magazine and put it in a nice gold frame. The picture showed a lady in a **fur** hat and a fur scarf. She sat straight, and she held up a big fur **muff**. Her arm up to the elbow was inside it. She held it up towards the person who looked at the picture.

Then Gregor looked out of the window. The weather was grey and dull. He could hear the rain hitting the glass, and this made him feel very sad. "Maybe I can sleep a little more and forget all this nonsense," he thought. But he could not do it. He always slept on his right side, and now he could not turn to that side. He threw himself onto his right side very hard, but every time he rolled back again.

He tried it maybe a hundred times. He closed his eyes, because he did not want to see his legs moving around. He stopped only when he felt a light, dull pain in his side. It was a new pain for him; he had never felt anything like it in his life.

"Oh God," he thought, "what a hard job I have chosen! Every day I travel, every day. This work on the road is much harder than work in the office at home. And there is the trouble with the trains, too. I always worry about catching them. The food is bad, and I never eat at the same time. I meet new people all the time, so I never really know anyone, and I have no friends. I hate it all!"

He felt a small **itch** high on his belly. Slowly he pushed himself on his back towards the top of the bed, so he could lift his head better. He found the place that itched. It was covered with small white spots, and he did not understand them. He wanted to touch the place with a leg. But when he touched it, he pulled the leg back at once, because suddenly he felt cold all over.

He slid back into his old position. "Getting up early every day makes you stupid," he thought. "A man needs enough sleep. Other salesmen live like kings. For example, sometimes I go back to the guest house in the morning to write out my new contracts. And these gentlemen are always still sitting there at their breakfast! If I did that, my **boss** would throw me out at once. But who knows? Maybe that would be good for me."

"I only stay in this job because of my parents. Without them, I would leave it. I wanted to leave a long time ago. I would go to the boss and tell him everything I think. I would tell him exactly how I feel. He would fall off his desk! It is a strange way to work, too. The boss sits high up at his desk and talks to his workers from up there. And you must go very close to him, because he does not hear well."

"But there is still hope. My parents owe the boss money, a big **debt**. I am saving money to pay it back. I think it will take five or six years. Then I will really go to the boss and tell him everything. That will be the big change in my life. But first I must get up. My train leaves at five."

Then he looked at the **alarm clock** on the **chest of drawers**. It was ticking quietly. "My God!" he thought. It was half past six, and the hands were still moving. It was even later than half past, almost quarter to seven. Hadn't the alarm clock rung? From the bed he could see that the alarm was set for four o'clock, and that was right. It must have rung. But how could he sleep through that loud noise? It was so loud that it shook the furniture! It was true that he had not slept peacefully. But maybe because of that he had slept more deeply.

What should he do now? The next train left at seven. To catch it, he would have to hurry like mad. But his samples were not in the bag yet. And he did not feel fresh or strong at all. Even if he caught the train, his boss would still be angry. The office boy was surely at the station at five o'clock, when Gregor's train left. He saw that Gregor was not on it. So he had probably told the boss about it long ago. This boy was the boss's man. He had no courage, and he was stupid.

What about saying he was **sick**? That was a bad idea, and people would not believe it. In five years of work Gregor had never been sick, not once. The boss would come to the house with the doctor from the **health insurance** company. He would say to his parents that their son was lazy. And he would agree with the doctor: Gregor was not sick. For this doctor, nobody was ever really sick, but many people were lazy and did not want to work. And in this case, would the doctor be completely wrong? Gregor felt well. He was only very sleepy, because he had slept so long. And he was much hungrier than usual.

He thought about all this very fast, but he still could not decide to get out of bed. Then the clock struck quarter to seven. Somebody knocked carefully on the door near his head. "Gregor," a voice said. It was his mother. "It's quarter to seven. Didn't you want to go somewhere?" Her voice was so soft! Gregor was shocked when he heard his own answer. It was hard to recognise his old voice in it. A painful **squeak** came from deep inside him, and he could not stop it. It was mixed with the words. At first you could hear the words, but then the sound made them unclear. A person could not be sure if he heard them right. Gregor had wanted to give a long answer and explain everything. But now he only said, "Yes, Mother, yes, thank you. I'm getting up now."

Through the wooden door, his mother probably did not hear the change in his voice. She was happy with his answer, and she walked away slowly. But because of this short talk, the rest of the family learned that Gregor was still at home. They did not expect it. Soon his father knocked on one of the side doors. He knocked softly, but with his fist. "Gregor, Gregor," he called, "what's the matter?" After a short time he called again, with a deeper, warning voice: "Gregor! Gregor!"

At the other side door his sister spoke in a sad, soft voice. "Gregor? Are you ill? Do you need anything?" Gregor answered both of them: "I'm ready now." He tried to make his voice normal. He spoke very carefully, and he made a long pause after each word. His father went back to his breakfast. But his sister whispered, "Gregor, please open the door. I'm asking you." Gregor did not even think about opening it. He was glad about his careful habit from his travels: at night he always **locked** all the doors, even at home.

First he wanted to get up in peace, without anybody disturbing him. He wanted to get dressed, and most of all he wanted to eat breakfast. After that he would think about the next thing. He knew that he could not think well in bed. He remembered that in the past he had often felt a small pain in bed. Maybe he had lain in a bad way. But later he had always seen that it was only his imagination. He was curious: how would today's strange ideas slowly go away? He was sure that his new voice was nothing serious. It was only the first sign of a bad cold. Travelling salesmen often get colds, because of their work.

It was easy to throw off the blanket. He only had to make himself a little bigger, and it fell down by itself. But then it was difficult, because he was so very wide. A man uses his arms and hands to push himself up. But Gregor only had all those little legs. They moved all the time in different directions, and he could not control them. When he tried to bend one leg, that leg was the first to stretch out. And when at last that leg did what he wanted, all the other legs were free. They moved around, and it hurt.
"I can't do this in bed," Gregor said to himself. "So I will not keep trying."

First he wanted to get the lower part of his body out of the bed. But he had never seen this part, and he could not imagine what it looked like. It was very hard to move, and it went so slowly. At last he was almost crazy. He pushed himself forward with all his strength, and he did not think. He went in the wrong direction, and he hit the bottom end of the bed very hard. It hurt like fire. From this pain he learned something. Maybe, at the moment, the lower part of his body felt pain more easily than any other part.

So he tried the other way. He wanted to get the top of his body out first, and he turned his head carefully to the side. This was quite easy. His body was wide and heavy, but slowly it followed his head. At last his head was out of the bed, in the fresh air. But then he had a thought. If he fell now, his head would almost surely be hurt. So he was afraid to go on in this way. And he could not hit his head and **lose consciousness** now, not for anything. It was better to stay in bed.

It was as hard to go back as it was to come out. He lay there and sighed. He watched his legs again. They fought against each other, even harder than before, if that was possible. He could not find any way to make peace and order in this chaos. He told himself again that he could not stay in bed. The best thing was to get out, whatever it cost. But he also remembered something: it was much better to think calmly than to do crazy things in a hurry.

At times like this he looked out of the window, as clearly as he could. But even the other side of the narrow street was hidden in the morning **fog**. The view did not give him any hope or joy. "Seven o'clock already," he said to himself when the clock struck again. "Seven o'clock, and there is still fog like this." He lay quietly for a little longer and breathed softly. Maybe he hoped that in this complete quiet everything would become real and normal again.

But then he said to himself, "Before quarter past seven, I must get out of the bed. I really must. And by then someone from the office will come to ask about me, because the office opens before seven." So he began to swing his whole long body out of the bed, all at once. If he fell out like this, and kept his head up, his head would probably stay safe. His back was hard, so he thought nothing would happen to it on the **carpet**. He was most afraid of the loud noise. He would surely make it, and the family would probably hear it through all the doors. They would be worried, or even afraid. But he had to take this risk.

Soon half of his body was out of the bed. This new way was more like a game than hard work. He only had to rock back and forth. Then he thought how simple everything would be if somebody helped him. Two strong people would be more than enough. He thought of his father and the maid. They would only have to put their arms under his round back and lift him out of the bed. Then they would bend down with him and wait, patient and careful, while he swung over onto the floor. There, he hoped, his little legs would be useful.

But should he really call for help? All the doors were locked, of course. But even without that, was it a good idea? Gregor was in a very bad situation, but he could not stop a smile when he thought of this.

After a while he was so far out of the bed that it was hard to keep his balance if he rocked too strongly. It was ten past seven. Very soon he had to make a final decision. Then somebody rang the bell at the door of the flat. "That's someone from the office," he said to himself, and he became very still. But his little legs only danced around even faster. For a moment everything was quiet. "They are not opening the door," Gregor thought, and he had a silly hope. But then the maid walked to the door with her strong steps, as always, and she opened it. Gregor heard the visitor's first words, and at once he knew who it was. It was the **manager** himself, the head clerk of the office.

Why was Gregor the only one with such bad luck? Why did he have to work for a company like this? Here they became **suspicious** at once, after the smallest mistake. Were all the workers bad? Was there not one good worker who was true to the company? A man who lost two hours of work one morning? Who felt so guilty about it that he went almost crazy? So crazy that he could not even get out of bed? Was it not enough to send a young helper to ask? If they really had to ask at all. Why did the manager come himself? Did they want to show the whole innocent family that this was very suspicious? So suspicious that only the manager was clever enough to look into it?

These thoughts upset Gregor. So he threw himself out of the bed with all his strength. It was not really a decision; he was simply upset. There was a loud bump, but it was not really a loud noise. The carpet made his fall softer. And his back was more elastic than he had thought, so the sound was dull and not very loud. But he had not held his head carefully enough. It hit the floor. He was angry, and it hurt. He turned his head and rubbed it on the carpet.

"Something has fallen down in there," said the manager in the room on the left. Gregor asked himself: could something like this happen to the manager one day? Something like the thing that happened to Gregor today? You had to agree that it was possible. But then, as if in a rough answer to this question, the manager walked a few strong steps in the next room. You could hear his shiny boots. From the room on the right Gregor's sister whispered, "Gregor, the manager is here." "Yes, I know," Gregor said to himself. But he did not dare to speak loudly enough for his sister to hear.

"Gregor," said his father from the room on the left, "the manager has come. He wants to know why you did not take the early train. We don't know what to tell him. And he wants to speak to you himself. So please open the door. I'm sure he will forgive the mess in your room."

"Good morning, Mr Samsa," the manager called. "He is not well," his mother said to the manager. At the same time his father was still talking through the door. "He is not well, please believe me," his mother went on. "Why else would Gregor miss a train? The boy only thinks about work. I am almost angry that he never goes out in the evening. He has been in town for a week now, and he has stayed at home every evening. He sits with us in the kitchen and reads the newspaper. Or he looks at the train timetables. For fun he works with his small **saw**. He made a little frame, for example. It only took him two or three evenings. You will be surprised, it is so nice! It is hanging in his room. You will see it when Gregor opens the door."

"Anyway, I'm very happy that you are here," his mother said. "Without you, we could not make Gregor open the door. He is so **stubborn**. And I am sure he is not well. This morning he said he was fine, but he is not."

"I'm coming in a moment," Gregor said slowly and carefully. He did not move, because he did not want to miss one word of the talk. "I can't explain it in any other way, Mrs Samsa," said the manager. "I hope it is nothing serious. But on the other hand, I must say this. We business people sometimes feel a little ill. But then we simply have to fight it, because of our work. Maybe that is lucky, maybe it is unlucky, as you like."

"Can the manager come in now?" his father asked, and he was impatient. He knocked on the door again. "No," said Gregor. In the room on the left there was an uncomfortable silence. In the room on the right his sister began to cry.

Why did his sister not go to the others? Maybe she had just got up, and she was not dressed yet. And why was she crying? Maybe because he had not got up, and he had not let the manager in. Maybe she was afraid that he would lose his job. Then the boss would ask their parents for the old debt again. But these were things for later, and there was no need to worry now.

Gregor was still there, and he did not want to leave his family at all. For now he just lay on the carpet. Nobody who knew his condition could seriously ask him to let the manager in. He was only a little impolite. Later he could easily find a good excuse. The boss could not fire him for this, not at once. It seemed to Gregor that it was much wiser to leave him alone now. That was better than talking to him and crying. But the others did not know what was happening. They were worried, so you could forgive their behaviour.

Now the manager spoke louder. "Mr Samsa," he called, "what is the matter? You lock yourself in your room. You only say yes or no. You make your parents worry very much, and there is no reason for it. And, I say this only by the way, you do not do your work. I have never seen anything like it. I speak now for your parents and for your boss. I must ask you for a clear and quick explanation. I am surprised, very surprised. I thought you were a calm and reasonable man. And now suddenly you behave in a strange way, for no reason."

"This morning your boss told me one possible reason why you did not come. It was about the company's money. A short time ago he gave you the job of collecting it from customers. But I almost gave him my **word of honour** that this was not the reason. Now I see how stubborn you are, and I don't understand it. I don't want to help you with the boss any more. And your job is not very safe anyway."

"I wanted to tell you all this in private, only to you. But you make me waste my time here for nothing. So why shouldn't your parents hear it, too? Your sales have been very bad lately. I know that it is not the time of year for good business. We understand that. But there is no time of year with no business at all, Mr Samsa. We can't allow it."

"But sir!" Gregor called. He was very excited and forgot everything else. "I will open the door now. Just a moment, please. I'm a little ill. I felt **dizzy** and I couldn't get up. I'm still in bed, but I feel fine again now. I'm getting out of bed right now. Please wait a little! It isn't as easy as I thought. But I'm all right now.

"It's terrible, what can happen to a person so suddenly! Last night I was fine. My parents know this, or maybe they know it better than I do. I felt a little strange last night already. They must have seen it. I don't know why I didn't tell the office! But we always think we can get over an illness without staying at home.

"Please, sir, don't make my parents suffer! You say bad things about my work, but they are not true. Nobody has ever said a word to me about them. Maybe you haven't read the new orders that I sent. And I will take the eight o'clock train, too. These few hours of rest have made me stronger. Please don't wait for me, sir. I will be at the office soon after you. Please tell this to the boss and speak well of me to him!"

Gregor poured out all these words and hardly knew what he was saying. At the same time he moved across the floor to the chest of drawers. This was easy, probably because he had already practised in bed. Now he tried to stand up against it.

He really wanted to open the door. He really wanted to let them see him and speak to the manager. The others were asking for it so strongly, and he wanted to know what they would say when they saw him. If they were shocked, it was no longer his fault, and he could rest. If they stayed calm, he had no reason to be upset either. And if he hurried, he could still be at the station by eight o'clock.

At first he slid down the smooth chest of drawers again and again. But then he gave himself one last push and stood upright. The lower part of his body hurt badly, but he didn't think about it any more. Next he let himself fall against the back of a chair near him. He held its edges tightly with his little legs. Now he was calmer, and he kept quiet. He wanted to hear what the manager was saying.
"Did you understand one word of that?" the manager asked his parents. "He isn't laughing at us, is he?"
"Oh, God!" called his mother. She was already crying. "Maybe he is very ill, and we are making him suffer!" Then she shouted, "Grete! Grete!"
"Mother?" his sister called from the other side. They were speaking across Gregor's room.
"You must go for the doctor now!" said his mother. "Gregor is ill. Quick, get the doctor! Did you hear how Gregor spoke just now?"
"That was the voice of an animal," said the manager. He said it very calmly, and this was very different from his mother's screams.

"Anna! Anna!" his father called through the hall to the maid in the kitchen. He clapped his hands. "Get a **locksmith**, now!" The two girls ran through the hall at once. Their skirts made a noise as they ran, and they pulled the front door of the flat open. How had his sister got dressed so fast? Gregor didn't hear the door close again. They had probably left it open. People often do this in a home where something terrible has happened.

But Gregor was much calmer now. So that was it: they could not understand his words any more. To him the words seemed clear, even clearer than before. Maybe his ears were used to the sound. But the people knew that something was wrong with him, and they wanted to help. Their first actions had been sure and wise, and this made him feel better.

He felt that he was back among people again. He expected great and wonderful things from the doctor and the locksmith, but he did not really see the difference between them. The next words would be very important. So he coughed a little to make his voice clear. But he was careful to cough quietly, because even his cough could sound different from a human cough. He was not sure that he could judge it himself any more.
Now it was very quiet in the next room. Maybe his parents were sitting at the table and whispering with the manager. Or maybe they were all pressing against the door and listening.

Gregor slowly pushed himself to the door with the chair. There he let go of the chair and threw himself against the door. He held himself up with the sticky ends of his little legs. He rested there for a short time after the hard work. Then he began to turn the **key** in the lock with his mouth.

Unfortunately he had no real teeth. So how could he hold the key? But he had a very strong **jaw**, and with it he really moved the key. He didn't think about it, but he was surely hurting himself. A brown liquid came out of his mouth, ran over the key and fell on the floor.
"Listen," said the manager in the next room. "He's turning the key."

This gave Gregor great hope. But all of them should have shouted to him, his father and mother too. "Well done, Gregor!" they should have cried. "Keep going! Hold the lock!" He imagined that they were all following his work with excitement. So he bit the key with all his strength and didn't care about the pain. When the key turned, he turned around the lock with it. He held himself up only with his mouth. He hung on the key, or he pushed it down again with the weight of his whole body, when it was needed.

Then he heard the clear sound of the lock opening. Now Gregor knew that he could stop and relax. He caught his breath and said to himself, "So I didn't need the locksmith after all." Then he put his head on the handle to open the door all the way.

He had to open the door like this, so it was already wide open before anyone could see him. It was a double door with two halves. First he had to turn himself slowly around one half. He had to be very careful, or he would fall on his back before he came into the room.

He was still busy with this hard movement and couldn't look at anything else. Then he heard the manager shout a loud "Oh!" It sounded like the wind. Now Gregor saw him too. He was the nearest to the door. He pressed his hand to his open mouth and slowly moved back. It looked as if a strong force that nobody could see was pushing him.

Gregor's mother was standing there. Her hair was still messy from bed, even with the manager there. She looked at his father. Her arms were crossed on her chest. Then she let them fall, took two steps towards Gregor, and sank down to the floor. Her skirts spread out around her, and her head sank down onto her chest.

His father looked angry. He made his hands into fists, as if he wanted to hit Gregor back into his room. Then he looked around the living room, unsure what to do. He covered his eyes with his hands and cried, and his big chest shook.

So Gregor did not go into the room. He leaned on the inside of the other half of the door, which was still locked. Only half of his body could be seen, and his head above it. He put his head on one side and looked at the others.

The day was now much lighter. Across the street there was a long, grey-black building. It was a **hospital**. Its hard, straight line of windows was clear to see. The rain was still falling, but now in big, single drops that hit the ground one by one.

The dishes from breakfast were on the table. There were many of them, because breakfast was the most important meal of the day for Gregor's father. He made it last for hours and read many different newspapers. On the wall exactly opposite was a photograph of Gregor from the army, when he was a **lieutenant**. He had his sword in his hand and a happy smile on his face. He wanted people to respect his uniform and the way he stood.
The door to the hall was open, and the front door of the flat was open too. So Gregor could see the **landing** and the top of the stairs going down.

"Now," said Gregor. He knew that he was the only one who was still calm. "I will get dressed right now, pack my samples and go. Will you please let me go? You can see, sir," he said to the manager, "that I'm not stubborn. I like my work. It is hard to be a travelling salesman, but without it I can't earn money.

"So where are you going? To the office? Yes? Will you tell them everything exactly as it is? A man can sometimes be unable to work. But that is the right time to remember what he did in the past. Later, when the problem is gone, he will work harder and think more about his work.

"You know very well that I owe a lot of money (a debt) to the boss. I must also look after my parents and my sister. So I'm in a difficult place, but I will work my way out of it again. Please don't make it harder for me than it is already. And please don't speak against me at the office. I know that nobody likes the salesmen. People think that we earn a huge amount of money and have an easy life. That is wrong, but they have no reason to think differently.

"But you, sir, you see more than the other workers. If I can say this just between us, you see more than the boss himself. It's easy for a businessman like him to make mistakes about his workers and to judge them too hard. And you know that we salesmen are away from the office almost all year. So people can easily talk badly about us, or something bad happens by chance, or they complain for no reason. It is almost impossible to defend ourselves. Usually we don't even hear about it. Or we hear only when we come home tired from a trip. Then we feel the bad results, and we don't know the cause.
"Please don't go away! First say something to show that I'm right, at least a little!"

But the manager turned away as soon as Gregor began to speak. He pushed out his lips and only looked back at Gregor over his shaking shoulders. While Gregor was speaking, he didn't stay still for a moment. He moved slowly towards the door and never took his eyes off Gregor.

He moved very slowly, as if there was a secret rule: "Do not leave this room." But when he reached the hall, he suddenly moved fast. He pulled his foot out of the living room and ran forward in a panic. In the hall he stretched out his right hand towards the stairs. It looked as if some magic force was waiting out there to save him.

Gregor understood that he could not let the manager go away in this mood. If he did, his place in the company would be in great danger. His parents didn't understand this very well. Over the years they had come to believe that this job would give Gregor money for his whole life. And now they had so many worries that they did not think about the future.

But Gregor thought about the future. He had to stop the manager, calm him down, make him believe Gregor and finally get him on Gregor's side. The future of Gregor and his family depended on it! If only his sister was here! She was clever. She had already started crying when Gregor was still lying quietly on his back. And the manager liked women. She could surely change his mind. She would close the front door in the hall and take away his fear. But his sister wasn't there, so Gregor had to do it himself.

He didn't stop to think about two things. He still didn't know how well he could move in this body. And people might not understand his words; probably they would not. He let go of the door and pushed himself through the opening. He wanted to reach the manager on the landing. The manager, in a silly way, was holding the **banister** with both hands. But Gregor fell at once. He gave a little scream, looked for something to hold, and landed on his many little legs.

Then, for the first time that day, he felt good in his body. His little legs stood on solid ground. To his joy, they did exactly what he wanted. They even tried to carry him where he wished to go. Soon he believed that all his troubles would be over at last. He stopped himself from walking, but he moved his body from side to side as he sat low on the floor.

His mother was not far in front of him. At first she seemed lost in her own thoughts. But then she suddenly jumped up with her arms out and her fingers wide. "Help! Please, help!" she shouted. She held her head as if she wanted to see Gregor better. But she was hurrying backwards without thinking, and this showed that she did not want to see him. She forgot that the table was behind her with all the breakfast things on it. When she reached the table, she sat down on it quickly and didn't know what she was doing. She didn't even seem to notice that she had knocked over the coffee pot, and coffee was running onto the carpet.

"Mother, Mother," said Gregor softly, and he looked up at her. For a moment he completely forgot about the manager. But when he saw the coffee, he couldn't stop himself. He bit at the air with his jaws. His mother screamed again. She ran away from the table and into the arms of his father, who was running towards her.

But Gregor had no time for his parents now. The manager was already on the stairs. His chin was on the banister, and he looked back one last time. Gregor ran towards him. He wanted to be sure to reach him. The manager must have expected something, because he jumped down several steps at once and disappeared. His shouts rang all around the stairway.

Unfortunately, when the manager ran away, Gregor's father panicked too. Until then he had been fairly calm. But now he did not run after the manager himself. He didn't even stay out of Gregor's way when Gregor ran after him. Instead, he took the manager's **stick** in his right hand. The manager had left it on a chair, with his hat and coat. With his left hand his father took a big newspaper from the table. With these he drove Gregor back into his room, and he **stamped** his foot at him.

Gregor asked his father to stop, but it didn't help. His father didn't understand him. Gregor bent his head down very politely, but his father only stamped harder. Across the room his mother opened a window, although the weather was cold. She leaned far out and pressed her hands to her face. A strong wind blew in from the street to the stairs. The curtains flew up, and the newspapers on the table moved. Some of them fell on the floor.

Nothing could stop his father. He drove Gregor back and made **hissing** noises like a wild man. But Gregor had never practised walking backwards before, so he could only go very slowly. If only he could turn round, he would be in his room at once. But he was afraid. If he took the time to turn, his father would lose patience. Any moment the stick in his father's hand could hit his back or head, and that could kill him.

But in the end Gregor saw that he had no choice. He saw, and he hated it, that he could not even go backwards in a straight line. So he began to turn round, as fast as he could. He kept looking at his father with fear. It went very slowly. Maybe his father saw that Gregor wanted to do the right thing, because he didn't stop him. Now and then he even used the end of his stick to show him, from far away, which way to turn.

If only his father would stop that terrible hissing! It made Gregor quite confused. He was almost round, but he still heard that hissing, and he made a mistake. He turned back a little the way he had come. He was happy when at last his head was in front of the doorway. But he saw that it was too narrow. His body was too wide to go through without trouble.

In this mood, of course, his father didn't think of opening the other half of the door to give Gregor enough space. He only had one idea: Gregor must go back into his room as fast as possible. He would never let Gregor get upright to prepare for the doorway. He made more noise than ever. He drove Gregor forward harder, as if nothing was in the way. To Gregor it sounded like there was more than one father behind him. It was not nice. Gregor pushed himself into the doorway, and he didn't care what happened.

One side of his body went up. He lay in the doorway on one side, not straight. His side rubbed hard against the white door and was badly hurt. It left ugly brown marks on the door. Soon he was stuck and couldn't move alone. The little legs on one side hung in the air and shook. The legs on the other side were pressed painfully to the floor.

Then his father gave him a hard push from behind. It freed him, and he flew deep into the room, **bleeding** a lot. His father banged the door shut with the stick. Then, at last, everything was quiet.

questions.q: True or false: Gregor woke up and found that he was a big insect.
questions.answer: True.

questions.q: Why were the doors of Gregor's room locked in the morning?
questions.answer: He always locked his doors at night. He learned to do this in hotels on his business trips.

questions.q: True or false: Gregor opened the door with his hands.
questions.answer: False. He turned the key with his mouth.

questions.q: Who came to Gregor's flat in the morning, and why?
questions.answer: The manager from his office came, because Gregor did not take the early train.

questions.q: What did the manager say about Gregor's work?
questions.answer: He said that Gregor's sales were bad and his job was not safe.

questions.q: True or false: The manager stayed in the flat and talked to Gregor.
questions.answer: False. He was afraid and ran away down the stairs.

questions.q: What did Gregor's father do when he saw Gregor in the living room?
questions.answer: He drove Gregor back into his room with a stick and a newspaper.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: It was almost dark that evening when Gregor woke up. His sleep was very deep, like the sleep of a sick man. He would have woken up soon anyway, even without any noise, because he had slept enough and felt rested. But he thought that a noise had woken him: some quick steps, and the sound of the door to the front room. Someone had closed it very carefully.

The light from the street lamps lay pale on the **ceiling** and on the tops of the furniture. But down on the floor, where Gregor was, it was dark. Slowly and clumsily he pushed himself to the door. He felt his way with his **antennae**, and he was only now learning how useful they were. He wanted to see what had happened there.

His whole left side felt like one long, painful **scar**. He moved badly on his two rows of little legs, like a man with a bad foot. One leg had been badly hurt that morning, when all those things happened. It was almost a miracle that only one leg was hurt. It dragged behind him, dead and useless.

When Gregor reached the door, he understood what had pulled him there. It was the smell of food. A **dish** stood by the door, full of sweet milk, with small pieces of white bread floating in it. He was so happy that he almost laughed. He was even hungrier than in the morning, so he put his head into the milk at once, almost up to his eyes.

But soon he pulled his head back, disappointed. First, his sore left side made eating hard. He could only eat if his whole body worked together, breathing noisily. Second, the milk did not taste good. Milk was usually his favourite drink, and surely his sister had put it there for that reason. But he turned away from the dish, almost against his will, and crawled back to the middle of the room.

Through the **crack** in the door Gregor could see that the gas lamp was on in the living room. At this time of day his father usually read the evening newspaper aloud to Gregor's mother, and sometimes to his sister. Now there was no sound at all. His sister often wrote to Gregor about this reading in her letters. But maybe his father had stopped doing it recently.

It was quiet everywhere, too, although surely somebody was in the flat. "What a quiet life our family has," Gregor said to himself. He looked into the dark and felt very proud. He was able to give his sister and his parents such a life, in such a nice home.
But what if all this peace, money and comfort came to a terrible end? Gregor did not want to think about that. So he began to move, and he crawled up and down the room.

During that long evening, one of the side doors opened a little and closed again quickly. Later the other side door did the same. It seemed that someone wanted to come in, but then changed their mind. Gregor went and waited by the door at once. He wanted to bring the shy visitor into the room somehow, or at least find out who it was. But the door did not open again that night. Gregor waited, but nobody came.

Earlier that morning, when the doors were locked, everybody had wanted to come in to him. Since then Gregor had opened one door himself, and somebody had clearly unlocked the other door during the day. But now nobody came in. And now the keys were on the outside of the doors.

The light in the living room went out only late at night. Now Gregor understood that his parents and his sister had been awake all evening. He could clearly hear all three of them walk away together on tiptoe. So nobody would come into his room until the morning. This gave Gregor plenty of time to think, quietly, about how he must change his life.

For some reason the tall, empty room felt strange to him. He lay flat on the floor and did not feel safe, although he had lived in this room for five years. He hardly knew what he was doing. He felt a little ashamed and hurried under the **couch**. The couch pressed a little on his back, and he could not lift his head. But at once he felt calm. He was only sorry that his body was too wide to go completely under it.

He stayed there all night. Sometimes he slept a little, but his hunger often woke him with a start. Sometimes he worried, and sometimes he had hopes, but they were not clear. But his thoughts always ended in the same way. For now he must stay calm. He must be patient and think very much about his family's feelings. Then his family could bear the trouble that he, in his present state, had to cause them.

Gregor soon had a chance to test how strong his decisions were. Early the next morning, when the night was almost over, his sister opened the door from the front room. She was almost fully dressed. She looked in with worried eyes. At first she did not see him. Then she saw him under the couch. (He had to be somewhere, for heaven's sake. He could not fly away.) She was so shocked that she lost control of herself. She shut the door hard again from outside.

But she seemed sorry for it. She opened the door again at once and came in on tiptoe. She walked like a person in the room of a very sick man, or of a stranger. Gregor had pushed his head forward to the edge of the couch, and he was watching her. Would she see that the milk was still there, not touched? Would she understand that it was not because he was not hungry? Would she bring him some other food that was better for him?

If she did not think of it herself, he would rather stay hungry than tell her. But he felt a terrible wish to run out from under the couch. He wanted to fall at his sister's feet and beg her for something good to eat. But his sister saw the full dish at once. A few drops of milk lay around it. She looked at it with surprise. She picked it up quickly, with a **rag** and not with her bare hands, and carried it out.

Gregor was very curious. What would she bring instead? He thought of many wild possibilities. But he could never have guessed what his kind sister really brought. To find out what he liked, she brought many different things. She spread them all out on an old newspaper. There were old vegetables that were half bad. There were bones from the evening meal, with white sauce that was hard now. There were a few **raisins** and **almonds**. There was some cheese. Two days earlier Gregor had said that nobody could eat it. There was a dry roll and some bread with butter and salt. She also put water in the dish, which was probably Gregor's dish from now on, and put it next to the food.

Then she thought about Gregor's feelings. She knew that he would not eat in front of her. So she hurried out and even turned the key in the lock. This was to show Gregor that he could make himself as comfortable as he liked. Gregor's little legs moved very fast. At last he could eat! His wounds seemed to be completely better, too, because moving was not hard for him now. This surprised him. More than a month before, when he was still a man, he had cut his finger a little with a knife. And that finger had still hurt the day before yesterday. "Do I feel less pain now than before?" he thought. And he was already sucking hungrily at the cheese. He wanted it at once, much more than the other foods on the newspaper.

One after another he ate the cheese, the vegetables and the sauce very fast, and his eyes were wet with pleasure. But he did not like the fresh food at all. He even dragged the things that he wanted to eat a little way away from them. He could not stand the smell of the fresh things.

Long after he had finished eating, he was still lying lazily in the same place. Then his sister slowly turned the key in the lock. It was a sign that he must go back and hide. He was half asleep, but he got a fright at once and hurried under the couch. But it was very hard to stay there, even for the short time that his sister was in the room. He had eaten so much that his body was now a little rounder. In the narrow space he could hardly breathe.

Almost without air, he watched with wide eyes. His sister, without thinking about it, took a **broom**. She swept up the leftovers. She also swept up the food that he had not touched at all, as if nobody could use it now. She quickly put everything into a **bin** and closed it with a wooden lid. Then she carried it all out. As soon as she turned her back, Gregor came out from under the couch and stretched his body.

This was how Gregor got his food every day now. The first time was in the morning, when his parents and the **maid** were still asleep. The second time was after the midday meal. Then his parents slept for a little while, and his sister sent the maid away to do something. His father and mother did not want him to die of hunger, of course. But maybe it was too much for them to know more about his eating. They could only bear to hear about it. And maybe his sister wanted to save them from more pain, because they were already suffering enough.

Gregor could never find out what the family had told the doctor and the **locksmith** that first morning, to send them away. Nobody could understand him. So nobody, not even his sister, thought that he could understand them. He had to be happy with only his sister's sighs and her prayers to the **saints** when she was in his room.

Later, she got a little more used to everything. Of course, she could never be completely used to it. Then Gregor sometimes heard a friendly word, or a word that he could understand as friendly. "He liked his dinner today," she sometimes said, when he had eaten all the food. When he left most of it, which happened more and more often, she often said sadly, "Now he has left everything again."

Gregor could not hear any news directly. But he heard a lot of what people said in the next rooms. When he heard voices, he ran to the right door and pressed his whole body against it. Almost every conversation was about him in some way, especially at first, even if they did not say it openly. For two whole days they talked at every meal about what they should do now. They talked about it between meals too, because at least two of the family were always at home. Nobody wanted to stay at home alone, and they could not leave the flat empty.

On the very first day the maid fell on her knees. She begged Gregor's mother to let her go at once. It was not clear how much she knew about what had happened. But she left in a quarter of an hour. She cried and thanked Gregor's mother for sending her away, as if it was a great favour. She also promised again and again that she would never tell anybody anything about it. Nobody had even asked her for that.

Now Gregor's sister also had to cook with his mother. This was not much trouble, because nobody ate very much. Gregor often heard one of them ask another to eat, but without success. The answer was always only "No, thank you, I have had enough," or something like it. Nobody drank much either.

His sister sometimes asked her father if he wanted a beer. She hoped that she could go and get it herself. When he did not answer, she said that she could send the woman who looked after their building for it. She said it so that he would not feel selfish. But then his father said a big, loud "No", and nothing more was said.

Before the first day was over, his father had explained everything about their money and their future to Gregor's mother and sister. Now and then he stood up from the table. He took a paper or a receipt out of the small **cash box**. Five years earlier his business had failed, and he had saved this box from it. Gregor heard him open the difficult lock. He took what he wanted and locked it again.

What Gregor heard now was the first good news for him since he was shut in his room. Until then he had believed that nothing was left from his father's business. At least, his father had never told him anything different. And Gregor had never asked him.

When the business failed back then, the family lost all hope. At that time Gregor only wanted to help them forget it as fast as possible. So he began to work very hard, with great fire. Almost overnight he changed from a simple clerk into a travelling **salesman**. As a salesman he could earn money in quite different ways. His work was a success, and Gregor turned this success straight into money. He put the money on the table at home, and his family was surprised and happy.

Those were good times. They never came again, at least not so beautifully. Later Gregor earned so much that he could pay for the whole family, and he did pay for it. They got used to it, both Gregor and the family. They took the money with thanks, and he gave it gladly. But they no longer gave him much warm love in return.

Only his sister was still close to Gregor. Unlike him, she loved music very much, and she played the **violin** beautifully, with deep feeling. Gregor had a secret plan. Next year he wanted to send her to the **conservatory**, although it would cost a lot of money. He would have to find that money in some other way.

Gregor was often away on his trips. During his short visits home, he and his sister often spoke about the conservatory. But it was always only a nice dream that could never come true. Their parents did not like to hear even this simple, harmless talk. But Gregor thought about it seriously. He decided to tell them his plan on Christmas Day, in a big, important speech.

These were the useless thoughts in Gregor's head now, while he stood up straight against the door and listened. Sometimes he was too tired to listen. His head fell tiredly against the door. Then he lifted it again with a start, because even a very small noise could be heard next door. And then everybody there went quiet. "What is he doing now?" his father said after a while. Clearly he had gone over to the door. Only then did the conversation slowly start again.

His father explained things many times. Partly this was because he had not dealt with money matters himself for a long time. Partly it was because Gregor's mother did not understand everything the first time. From these explanations Gregor learned something that made him glad. Some money was still left from the old days, in spite of all their bad luck. It was not much. But nobody had touched it all these years, so some **interest** had grown on it. Also, every month Gregor brought his money home and kept only a little for himself. The family had not spent all of it, so this money had grown too.

Behind the door Gregor nodded happily. He had not expected this. He was glad that his father was so careful and had saved the money. He could have used this extra money to pay back part of his father's **debt** to his boss. Then the day when he could leave his job would have come much sooner. But now it was certainly better the way his father had done it.

But this money was not enough. The family could not live only on the interest. The money was enough for maybe one year, or two years, not more. So it was money that they should not really touch. They should keep it for an emergency. Money for living had to be earned.

His father was healthy, but he was old. He did not believe in himself. For the last five years he had not worked. It was the first holiday in a life full of trouble and no success. He had become very fat, slow and clumsy.
Would Gregor's old mother have to earn money now? She had **asthma**. Even to walk through the flat was hard for her. Every second day she lay on the sofa by the open window and fought for air.

Would his sister have to earn money? She was still a child, only seventeen. Until then her life had been easy and pleasant, and many girls could envy it. She wore nice clothes, slept late, helped in the house, and had a few small pleasures. Most of all she played the violin.
When they began to talk about the need to earn money, Gregor always moved away from the door first. Then he threw himself on the cool leather sofa next to it. He felt hot with shame and sadness.

He often lay there all night. He did not sleep at all, but scratched the leather for hours. Or he made a great effort. He pushed a chair to the window and climbed up onto the window **sill**. Then, with the chair under him for support, he leaned on the window and looked out. When he was still a man, this had always given him a great feeling of freedom. Now it was more a memory than a real feeling. Every day he saw things less clearly, even things that were quite near.

Earlier he had often said bad words about the hospital across the street, because he saw it all the time. Now he could not see it at all. He knew that he lived in Charlottenstrasse, a quiet street, although it was in the middle of the city. Without this knowledge, he could think that he was looking out of his window at an empty desert. There the grey sky and the grey earth became one.

His sister was clever and watched carefully. She only needed to see the chair by the window twice. After that, every time she cleaned the room, she pushed the chair back to the window, to the same place. And from then on she left the inner window open.

If Gregor could only speak to his sister, he could thank her for everything she did for him. Then it would be easier for him to bear it. But he could not, and this hurt him. His sister, of course, tried not to show how hard it was for her. The longer it lasted, the better she could do it. But with time Gregor also saw through everything much better.

It was now very unpleasant for him whenever she came in. She closed the door at once, so that nobody would have to see into Gregor's room. Then she went straight to the window and opened it quickly, almost as if she could not breathe. Even when it was cold, she stayed at the window for a little while and breathed deeply.

Twice a day she frightened Gregor with this running and noise. He shook under the couch all that time. He knew very well that she would gladly have saved him from this. But she could not stay in the same room with him when the windows were closed.

About a month had passed since Gregor's change. His sister had no real reason now to be shocked by the way he looked. But one day she came into the room a little earlier than usual. She found him still looking out of the window, without moving. He was exactly where he looked most terrible.

If she simply did not come in, that was no surprise for Gregor. She could not open the window at once while he was standing there. But she did more than stay out. She stepped back at once and shut the door behind her. A stranger would have thought that Gregor had attacked her and tried to bite her.

Of course Gregor went at once and hid under the couch. But he had to wait until midday before his sister came back. She seemed much more nervous than usual. So he understood that she still could not bear the sight of him. And this would not change. She probably had to fight her wish to run away. She felt it even when she saw only the small part of him that stuck out from under the couch.

One day he wanted to save her even from this sight. It took him four hours. He carried the **bedsheet** on his back to the couch and put it there, so that it covered him completely. Now his sister could not see him, even if she bent down. If she did not think the **sheet** was needed, she could simply take it away. It was clear, after all, that Gregor did not hide himself so completely for pleasure.
She left the sheet where it was. Once Gregor carefully looked out from under the sheet to see how his sister liked the new arrangement. He thought that he saw a thankful look in her eyes.

For the first two weeks, Gregor's parents did not have the courage to come into his room to see him. He often heard them talk about Grete. They said how much they liked all her new work. Before, they had thought she was a girl who was not very useful, and they had often been angry with her.

Now both parents often waited outside Gregor's door while Grete cleaned his room. When she came out, she had to tell them everything. How did the room look? What did Gregor eat? How did he behave this time? Was he a little better, maybe?

His mother wanted to visit Gregor quite soon. But his father and Grete told her not to, and at first she agreed. Gregor listened carefully to all this, and he thought they were right. Later they had to **hold back** Gregor's mother by force. She cried, "Let me go and see Gregor! He is my poor son! Don't you understand? I must see him!"

Then Gregor thought that maybe it would be better if his mother came in. Not every day, of course, but once a week, perhaps. She could understand everything much better than Grete. Grete was brave, but she was still only a child. Maybe she did not really understand how hard her job was.

Gregor soon got his wish to see his mother. He did not want to upset his parents. So in the daytime he did not go to the window, where people could see him. And the floor was small, and he had little room to crawl. It was hard to lie quietly all night. Soon he did not enjoy his food at all. So, to have some fun, he began to crawl up and down the walls and the ceiling.

He liked hanging from the ceiling best. It was very different from lying on the floor. He could breathe more easily, and his body moved a little, like a swing. Up there he felt relaxed and almost happy. Sometimes he even surprised himself: he let go of the ceiling and fell down to the floor with a bang. But now he controlled his body much better than before. Even after a big fall like that, he was not hurt.

Very soon Grete saw Gregor's new game. His feet had left sticky marks on the walls when he crawled. She decided to make crawling as easy as possible for him. She wanted to take away the furniture that was in his way, most of all the **chest of drawers** and the **desk**. But she could not do it alone. She did not dare to ask her father for help. The maid was only sixteen years old. The cook had left. Since then the maid had worked bravely, but she certainly would not help with this. She had even asked to keep the kitchen door locked all the time and to open it only for something very important. So Grete had no choice. She waited for a time when her father was not at home, and then she asked her mother to help.

Gregor heard his mother call out happily as she came near. But at the door she became silent. First Grete came in alone and looked around the room to check that everything was all right. Only then did she let her mother in. Before they came, Gregor had quickly pulled the sheet lower over the couch and had made more folds in it. Now it really looked as if someone had thrown it there by chance. This time Gregor did not look out from under the sheet. He decided to see his mother later, not now. He was just happy that she had come. "Come in, you can't see him," said Grete. Clearly she was leading her mother in by the hand.

The old chest of drawers was too heavy for two weak women. Gregor listened while they pushed it away from its place. Grete took the heaviest work for herself, and she did not listen when her mother said, "Be careful, you will hurt yourself." It took a very long time. After fifteen minutes or more, his mother said they should leave the chest where it was. First, it was too heavy. They could not finish before Gregor's father came home. And if they left the chest in the middle of the room, it would be even more in Gregor's way. Second, she was not sure that taking the furniture away would really help Gregor.

She thought the opposite. The empty walls made her feel sad in her heart. Why would Gregor feel different? He had lived with this furniture for a long time, and he was used to it. In an empty room he would feel alone and forgotten.

Then she spoke very quietly, almost in a whisper. She did not know where Gregor was, and she did not want him to hear even her voice. She was sure that he did not understand her words. She said, "If we take the furniture away, it will look like we have lost all hope that he will get better. It will look like we are leaving him alone, and he must help himself. I think it is better to keep the room just as it was. Then, when Gregor comes back to us, he will find everything the same. And it will be easier for him to forget the time in between."

When Gregor heard his mother's words, he understood something. For two months nobody really talked to him, and the family's life was always the same. This must have made his mind confused. He could find no other reason why he had seriously wanted his room to be empty.

Had he really wanted to turn his warm room, with its nice furniture from his family, into a **cave**? Then he could crawl around in every direction without any problem. But he would also quickly forget that he had once been a human. He was already very close to forgetting. He had not heard his mother's voice for a long time. Only her voice had woken him up.

Nothing should be taken away. Everything had to stay. The furniture was good for him, and he needed it. And if it was difficult for him to crawl around without thinking, that was not bad. It was very good.

But, sadly, Grete did not agree. In these weeks she had got used to a new idea, and she had some reason for it. She believed that she was the one who spoke to their parents for Gregor, in everything about him. So her mother's advice was now enough reason for Grete to want even more. At first she had wanted to take away only the chest and the desk. Now she wanted to take away all the furniture. Only the couch, the most important thing, could stay.

It was not just a child's wish to have her own way. It was not only her new confidence either. She really saw that Gregor needed a lot of room to crawl. And, as far as anyone could see, the furniture was no use to him at all. But girls of her age get excited about things. They want to do what they like, whenever they can. Maybe this was why Grete wanted to make Gregor's situation look worse than it was. Then she could do even more for him. Perhaps only Grete would dare to enter a room where Gregor crawled alone on the empty walls.

So Grete did not listen to her mother. Her mother already looked nervous in Gregor's room. Soon she stopped talking and helped Grete to push out the chest of drawers with all her little strength. Gregor could live without the chest if he had to. But the writing desk had to stay.

The two women pushed the chest out of the room. It was hard, and they made heavy, tired sounds. As soon as they did this, Gregor put his head out from under the couch to see what he could do. He wanted to be careful and kind. But, unfortunately, his mother came back first. Grete was in the next room. She held the chest in her arms. She pulled and pushed it from side to side alone, but of course it did not move at all.

His mother was not used to seeing Gregor. The sight of him could make her ill. So Gregor ran backwards to the far end of the couch. But he was frightened, and he could not stop the sheet at the front from moving a little. That was enough. His mother noticed it. She stood very still for a moment. Then she went back out to Grete.

Gregor said to himself again and again that nothing special was happening. They were only moving some furniture, that was all. But soon he had to be honest with himself. The women walked to and fro. They called short words to each other. The furniture made a loud noise on the floor. All this felt to him like an attack from every side.

He pulled in his head and his legs and pressed his body to the floor. He knew that he could not stand this much longer. They were emptying his room. They were taking away everything he loved. They had already taken out the chest with his **fretsaw** and his other tools. Now they wanted to take the writing desk. It had stood in one place for so long that there was a clear mark in the floor. He had done his homework at that desk when he was a business student. He had also done it there at high school, and even in his first years at school. He really could not wait any longer to see if the two women meant well.
Anyway, he had almost forgotten that they were there. They were too tired to talk while they worked. He could only hear their heavy feet on the floor.

The women were leaning on the desk in the other room and resting. Gregor rushed out, and he changed direction four times. He did not know what to save first. Then he saw the picture on the wall. The wall was already empty and the picture was alone there. It was the picture of the lady in **fur**. She wore a lot of fur.

He quickly climbed up onto the picture and pressed himself against its glass. The glass held him well, and it felt good on his hot belly. At least this picture was safe now. Gregor covered all of it, and nobody would take it away. He turned his head towards the living room door. He wanted to watch the women when they came back.

The women did not rest for long, and they came back soon. Grete had her arm around her mother and almost carried her. "What shall we take now?" said Grete, and she looked around. Then her eyes met Gregor's eyes on the wall.

Maybe she stayed calm only because her mother was there. She bent her face to her mother, so that her mother would not look around. She spoke quickly, and her voice shook. "Come on, let's go back to the living room for a little while." Gregor understood her plan. She wanted to take her mother to a safe place. Then she wanted to chase him down from the wall. Well, let her try! He sat on his picture and did not move. He would rather jump at Grete's face.

But Grete's words made her mother afraid. She stepped to one side and saw something huge and brown on the flowers of the **wallpaper**. Before she understood that it was Gregor, she screamed, "Oh God, oh God!" She threw out her arms and fell onto the couch, as if she had given up on everything. She lay there and did not move.

"Gregor!" shouted Grete. She looked at him angrily and shook her fist. It was the first word she had said directly to him since his change. She ran into the other room to get some medicine to wake her mother. Gregor wanted to help too. He could save his picture later. But he was stuck to the glass, and he had to pull himself off with force. Then he ran into the next room too, as if he could give his sister advice like in the old days. But he could only stand behind her and do nothing.

She was looking at different bottles. When she turned around, he frightened her. A bottle fell on the floor and broke. A small piece of glass cut Gregor's face. Some strong medicine splashed all over him, and it burned. Grete did not wait any longer. She took as many bottles as she could and ran to her mother. She pushed the door shut with her foot.

Now Gregor was shut out from his mother. Maybe she was near death, and it was because of him. He could not open the door, because he did not want to chase his sister away. And she had to stay with their mother. He could only wait. He felt afraid and guilty, and he began to crawl about. He crawled over everything, the walls, the furniture and the ceiling. At last the whole room began to turn around him. He was so confused that he fell down onto the middle of the dining table.

He lay there for a while. He could not feel anything and did not move. Everything around him was quiet. Maybe that was a good sign. Then somebody came to the door. Of course, the maid was locked in her kitchen, so Grete had to go and open it. It was his father. He had come home.

"What has happened?" were his first words. Grete's face must have told him everything. She answered in a low voice, and she pressed her face against his chest. "Mother **fainted**, but she is better now. Gregor got out." "I knew it," said his father. "I always said so, but you women never listen."

Gregor understood that Grete had not said enough. His father thought something bad had happened, and that Gregor had done something violent. So now Gregor had to calm his father down. He had no time to explain, and it was not possible anyway. So he ran to the door of his room and pressed himself against it. He wanted his father to see this at once when he came in from the hall: Gregor meant well. He wanted to go back into his room immediately. They did not have to chase him. They only had to open the door, and he would disappear.

But his father was not in the mood to see small things like that. "Ah!" he shouted when he came in. He sounded angry and glad at the same time. Gregor pulled his head back from the door and lifted it towards his father.

He had never imagined his father like this. Lately he had spent all his time crawling around. So he had not watched the rest of the flat as before. He should have known that things had changed. But still, was this really his father? Before, his father was a tired man. He lay in bed, almost buried, when Gregor came back from a business trip. In the evening he received Gregor in an armchair in his nightgown. He could hardly stand up. To show his joy, he only lifted his arms. A few times a year, on a Sunday or a holiday, they went for a walk together. His father walked between Gregor and his mother, in a thick overcoat. He was always a little slower than they were, and they already walked slowly for him. He put his stick down carefully. When he wanted to say something, he always stopped and called the others around him.

Now he stood up straight. He wore a smart blue **uniform** with gold buttons, like the ones bank workers wear. Above the high, stiff collar of the coat, his strong double chin showed. Under his thick **eyebrows** his dark eyes looked sharp and awake. His white hair was usually untidy, but now it was combed very flat against his head.

He took his cap, which had gold letters on it, maybe from a bank. He threw it across the room, and it flew in an arc onto the sofa. He put his hands in his trouser pockets and pushed back his long coat. With a hard face, he walked towards Gregor. He probably did not know himself what he wanted to do. But he lifted his feet unusually high. Gregor was amazed at the huge **soles** of his boots. But he did not waste time on that. He had known it from the first day of his new life: his father thought he must always be very strict with him.

So Gregor ran in front of his father. When his father stopped, he stopped. When his father moved, even a little, he hurried forward again. They went round the room many times, and nothing important happened. It did not even look like a chase, because everything was so slow. Gregor stayed on the floor all the time. He was afraid that his father would get even angrier if he ran onto the wall or the ceiling.

But Gregor knew that he could not run like this for long. For each of his father's steps, he had to make very, very many movements. He was soon out of breath. Even in his old life, his lungs had not been very strong. Now he rushed from side to side to find all his strength for running. He could hardly keep his eyes open. His thoughts were too slow, and he could think of no other way to save himself than running. He almost forgot that he could use the walls. But here the walls were hidden behind carefully carved furniture, full of sharp corners and points.

Then something flew down right beside him. Someone threw it lightly, and it rolled in front of him. It was an **apple**. Another apple flew at him at once. Gregor stopped in shock. Running was no use now, because his father had decided to throw things at him. His father had filled his pockets with fruit from the bowl on the **sideboard**. Now he threw one apple after another, and he did not take time to aim well.

The small red apples rolled on the floor and hit each other, as if they had little electric motors. One apple, thrown without much force, touched Gregor's back and slid off. It did not hurt him. But the next apple came right after it and hit him hard. It got stuck in his back. Gregor wanted to drag himself away. He thought the strange, terrible pain might go away if he changed his place. But he felt nailed to the floor. He spread out his body, and all his senses were confused.

The last thing he saw was this. The door of his room opened, and Grete was screaming. His mother ran out in front of her, in her blouse. When her mother fainted, Grete had taken off some of her mother's clothes, so that her mother could breathe more easily. His mother ran to his father. Her skirts were not tied, and they fell one after another to the floor. She almost fell over the skirts, but she pushed herself to his father. She put her arms around him and held him close, as if they were one person. Then Gregor could not see anything. Her hands were behind his father's head, and she begged him to let Gregor live.

questions.q: True or false: Gregor drank all the milk and liked it.
questions.answer: False. He did not like the milk, and he left it.

questions.q: True or false: Grete brought many kinds of food on an old newspaper.
questions.answer: True. There were old vegetables, bones, cheese, bread and more.

questions.q: Why did Grete and the parents not want to see Gregor eat?
questions.answer: Grete knew that Gregor did not want to eat in front of her. For the parents it was too hard to see, and Grete wanted to protect them from more pain.

questions.q: What was Gregor's secret plan for Grete?
questions.answer: He wanted to send her to the conservatory next year and tell everyone on Christmas Day.

questions.q: Why did Gregor carry a sheet to the sofa?
questions.answer: He wanted to hide completely, so that Grete did not have to see him.

questions.q: Why did Grete want to take the furniture out of the room?
questions.answer: She wanted to give Gregor more room to crawl, and she wanted to do more for him.

questions.q: True or false: Gregor's father was kind to him when he came home.
questions.answer: False. He was angry, and he threw apples at Gregor.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Nobody dared to take the **apple** out of Gregor's back. It stayed there in his body, and everyone could see it. Gregor had lived with this **injury** for more than a month. It was so serious that it reminded even his father of one thing. Gregor's body was now sad and horrible to look at, but he was still a member of the family. You could not treat him like an enemy. The family had a duty to hide their **disgust** and to be patient. Only patient, nothing more.

Because of the injury, Gregor could not move well any more, and maybe he never would again. He was now like an old **invalid**. It took him many long minutes to cross his room. Climbing on the ceiling was not possible now. But in Gregor's opinion, one new thing was worth all this. Every evening the family left the door to the living room open. Soon it became his habit to watch the door carefully for one or two hours before they opened it. Then he lay in the dark of his room, where nobody in the living room could see him. He watched the family in the light of the dinner table and listened to their talk. Everyone allowed it, in a way. It was very different from before.

Of course, the family did not have lively talks any more. In the old days, Gregor always thought of those talks and missed them. He did it when he was tired and climbed into a damp bed in some small hotel room. Now it was mostly quiet. Soon after dinner his father fell asleep in his chair. His mother and sister told each other to be quiet. His mother sat bent low under the lamp and **sewed** fine underwear for a fashion shop. His sister now had a job in a shop, and in the evenings she learned **shorthand** and French. She hoped to get a better job one day. Sometimes his father woke up and said to his mother, "You are sewing so much again today!" He spoke as if he did not know that he had been asleep. Then he slept again, and the mother and sister looked at each other with tired smiles.

His father was **stubborn**. He did not want to take off his **uniform**, even at home. His **nightgown** hung on its hook and nobody used it. The old man slept in his chair, fully dressed. It was as if he was always ready to work. He seemed to wait for his boss's voice, even here. The uniform was not new even at the start. And because he slept in it, it slowly became more and more **shabby**. His mother and sister tried to take care of it, but it did not help. Gregor often looked at it for a whole evening. It was covered with **stains**, but the gold buttons were always clean and bright. In this coat the old man slept, not comfortable at all, but calm.

When the clock struck ten, Gregor's mother woke his father with soft words. She tried to make him go to bed. He could not sleep well in the chair. He needed his sleep because he had to get up at six for work. But since he had started work again, he was more stubborn. He always wanted to stay at the table longer, although he fell asleep every time. Then it was harder than ever to get him from the chair to his bed. His wife and daughter complained a little and warned him. But he only shook his head slowly for a quarter of an hour. His eyes stayed closed and he did not get up. His mother pulled his **sleeve** and whispered kind words in his ear. His sister left her work and came to help. But nothing worked, and he just sank deeper into the chair. Only when the two women took him under the arms did he suddenly open his eyes. He looked at one woman, then at the other, and said, "What a life! Is this the peace I get in my old age?" Then, with the two women holding him, he slowly and carefully stood up, as if he was carrying a very heavy load. They took him to the door. There he sent them away and walked on alone. But his mother quickly threw down her needle. His sister threw down her pen. They ran after him to help him again.

Who in this tired family, where everyone worked too much, had time to care for Gregor more than they really had to? The family had less and less money. So they sent the maid away. Now a very big **cleaning woman** with strong bones and white hair, which flew around her head, came every morning and evening. She did the heaviest work. His mother did everything else, and she also did a lot of sewing. In the evenings they talked about the price they had hoped to get. From these talks Gregor even learned that they had sold some of the family's **jewellery**. And his mother and sister had always loved wearing it at parties and celebrations. But the biggest complaint was about the flat. It was much too big for them now, but they could not leave it. They could not think of a way to move Gregor to a new home. Gregor saw clearly that he was not the only reason. It would be easy to move him in a box with a few holes for air. The real reason was their **despair**. They felt that nobody they knew, and nobody in their family, had ever had such bad luck. The family did everything the world asks from poor people. His father brought breakfast to people who worked in a bank. His mother gave all her strength to washing clothes for strangers. His sister ran back and forth behind her desk when customers called her. But they had no more strength to do anything else. And the injury in Gregor's back started to hurt as much as on the first day. After they had put his father to bed, his mother and sister came back. They left their work and sat close together, cheek to cheek. His mother pointed at Gregor's room and said, "Close that door, Grete." Then Gregor was in the dark again. In the next room the two women cried, and their tears mixed together. Or they just sat and looked at the table with dry eyes.

Gregor hardly slept at all, not at night and not in the day. Sometimes he thought that the next time the door opened he would take charge of the family's affairs again, like before. He had long forgotten his boss and the **manager**, but now they came back into his thoughts. He thought of the salesmen and the **apprentices**, and of the stupid boy who brought tea. He thought of two or three friends from other businesses. He remembered a maid in a hotel in the country, a sweet memory that came and went. He remembered a **cashier** in a hat shop. He liked her and was serious about her, but he was too slow. All these people came to his mind, mixed with strangers and with people he did not remember any more.
