But they did not help him or his family. He could not reach any of them, and he was glad when they went away. At other times he did not want to care about his family at all. He was full of anger because nobody paid attention to him. He could not think of anything he wanted. But he made plans to go into the **pantry**. He wanted to take all the food he had a right to, even when he was not hungry. His sister did not think about how to please him any more. In the morning and at midday, before she ran to work, she quickly pushed some food into his room with her foot. In the evening she swept it out with a **broom**. She did not care if he ate it or not. Most of the time he did not touch it. She still cleaned his room in the evening, but now she did it as fast as she could. There were dirty marks on the walls, and here and there were little balls of dust and dirt. At first, when his sister came in, Gregor went to one of the worst places. He wanted to show her that she did a bad job. But he could stay there for weeks, and she would do nothing about it. She saw the dirt as well as he did, but she decided to leave it there. At the same time she became sensitive in a new way, and the whole family understood it. Cleaning Gregor's room was her job, only hers. Once his mother cleaned the room very well. She needed several **buckets** of water. But all that water made Gregor ill, and he lay flat on the couch, angry and sad, without moving. His mother was punished even more for this. In the evening, as soon as his sister came home, she saw the change in Gregor's room. She was very hurt and ran into the living room. His mother raised her hands and begged her, but his sister burst into wild tears. His father jumped up from his chair in fright, and the two parents looked at her, surprised and helpless. Then they too became upset. His father, standing on his mother's right, blamed her. He said she should have left the cleaning of Gregor's room to his sister. On her left, his sister screamed that her mother must never clean Gregor's room again. His mother tried to pull his father into the bedroom, because he was wild with anger. His sister shook with tears and hit the table with her small fists. And Gregor hissed with anger, because nobody even thought of closing his door. Then he would not have to see all this and hear the noise.

Gregor's sister was tired from her work outside, and taking care of Gregor like before was even more work. But even so, his mother should not do this work for her. And they must not forget about Gregor either. Now there was the cleaning woman. She was an old **widow**. Her strong bones helped her to survive the hardest things in her long life, and Gregor did not really disgust her. One day she opened the door of Gregor's room, just by chance and not because she was curious. She found herself face to face with him. He was very surprised. Nobody was running after him, but he began to run back and forth. The woman just stood there amazed, with her hands folded in front of her. After that she always opened the door a little every evening and every morning to look at him for a moment. At first she also called to him. She used words that she probably thought were friendly. "Come here, you old **dung-beetle**!" she said, or "Look at the old dung-beetle!" Gregor never answered when she spoke like this. He stayed where he was and did not move, as if the door had never opened. Why didn't they tell her to clean his room every day? Then she would not annoy him for no reason, whenever she liked. One early morning, heavy rain hit the windows. Maybe it was a sign that spring was coming. The woman began to talk to him in that way again. Gregor was so angry that he turned and went toward her. He was slow and weak, but it was like an attack. The woman was not afraid. She lifted a chair that stood near the door and stood there with her mouth wide open. She clearly meant to keep her mouth open until the chair in her hand came down on Gregor's back. "So you are not coming closer?" she asked, when Gregor turned round again. And she calmly put the chair back in the corner.

Gregor almost stopped eating. He only took a little food into his mouth when he happened to be near it. He played with it and kept it there for a few hours, and most of the time he spat it out again. At first he thought he could not eat because he was sad about the state of his room. But he had soon got used to the changes. The family now put things in his room that they had no place for anywhere else. There were many such things now, because one room in the flat was rented to three men, the three **lodgers**. These serious men all had full **beards**, as Gregor saw one day through the crack in the door. They were terribly strict about order, and everything had to be tidy. They wanted it not only in their own room. Because they rented a room here, they wanted it in the whole flat, and most of all in the kitchen. They could not stand **clutter**, and above all dirty clutter. They had also brought most of their own furniture and things. So many things in the flat were not needed any more. The family could not sell them, but did not want to throw them away. All these things went into Gregor's room. The dustbins from the kitchen went there too. The cleaning woman was always in a hurry. Everything she could not use at the moment, she just threw into his room. Luckily, Gregor usually saw only the thing and the hand that held it. Maybe she wanted to take the things out again when she had time, or throw everything away at once. But in fact the things stayed where they fell, unless Gregor crawled through the rubbish and moved them. At first he moved them because he had to, as he had no free place to crawl. Later he began to like it. But after this crawling he was sad and tired to death, and he did not move for hours.

Sometimes the lodgers ate their evening meal at home, in the living room that everyone used. So the door to this room was often closed in the evening. But Gregor easily accepted that the door was closed. On many evenings the door had been open, but he had not used it. He had lain in the darkest corner of his room, and the family had not noticed it. But one time the cleaning woman left the living room door a little open. It stayed open when the lodgers came in that evening and somebody turned on the light. They sat down at the table, where Gregor used to eat with his father and mother in the old days. They opened their **napkins** and took their knives and forks. At once Gregor's mother came to the door with a dish of meat. His sister came right behind her with a dish full of potatoes. The food was hot, and its smell filled the room. The lodgers bent over the dishes in front of them, as if they wanted to test the food before eating. The man in the middle seemed to be the boss of the other two. He cut a piece of meat while it was still in the dish. He clearly wanted to know if it was cooked enough or if they should send it back to the kitchen. He was happy with it. Gregor's mother and sister were watching with worry. Now they could breathe again, and they smiled.

The family ate in the kitchen. But before going there, Gregor's father came into the living room. He bowed once with his cap in his hand and walked around the table. The lodgers all stood up together and said something into their beards. Then they were alone and they ate almost without a word. Gregor thought it was strange. Over all the noises of eating, he could still hear their teeth chewing. It was as if they wanted to show him that you need teeth to eat. Even the nicest **jaws** could do nothing without teeth. "I want to eat something," said Gregor, worried, "but not this kind of food. These lodgers eat so well! And I am dying here!"

Gregor could not remember hearing the **violin** in all that time. But this evening it began to play in the kitchen. The three lodgers had already finished their meal. The one in the middle had taken out a newspaper and given a page to each of the others. Now they leaned back in their chairs, reading and smoking. When the violin began to play, they listened. They stood up and went on tiptoe to the door of the hall, and stood there close together. Somebody in the kitchen must have heard them, because Gregor's father called, "Maybe the music is not nice for the gentlemen? We can stop it at once." "On the contrary," said the middle lodger. "Would the young lady like to come and play here in the room for us? It is much more comfortable and pleasant here." "Oh yes, we would love to!" Gregor's father called back, as if he was the player himself. The lodgers went back into the room and waited. Soon his father came with the **music stand**, his mother with the music, and his sister with the violin. She calmly got everything ready to play. It was the first time that his parents had rented out a room, so they were much too polite to the lodgers. They did not even dare to sit on their own chairs. His father leaned against the door, with his right hand between two buttons of his uniform coat. One of the lodgers offered his mother a chair. He put it down in a corner, away from everyone, just by chance. She did not move it and sat there.

His sister began to play. His father and mother, one on each side, watched her hands closely. The music pulled Gregor in, and he dared to come forward a little. His head was already in the living room. Before, he had been proud that he always thought of others. Now he hardly noticed that he did not think of them any more. And he had even more reason to hide now. He was covered with dust from his room. The dust lay everywhere there and flew up at the smallest movement. He carried threads, hairs and bits of food on his back and sides. He did not care about anything now. Before, he used to lie on his back and clean himself on the carpet several times a day. Now he did not do it any more. But even like this, he was not shy to go a little way onto the clean floor of the living room.

But nobody saw him. The family was fully busy with the violin. At first the three lodgers, with their hands in their pockets, stood much too close behind the music stand. They wanted to see every note. Surely this disturbed Gregor's sister. But soon they moved back to the window, with their heads low, and talked quietly together. The family stayed near the music, but the lodgers stayed at the window, and Gregor's father watched them with worry. Now it was clear: they had wanted to hear beautiful or interesting music, but had been disappointed. They were tired of the whole thing. Now they let it disturb their peace only to be polite. It was especially unpleasant how they all blew the smoke of their **cigarettes** up from their mouths and noses. And yet Gregor's sister played so beautifully. Her head leaned to one side, and her eyes followed the notes with a careful, sad look. Gregor crawled a little farther. He kept his head low to the floor, so he could meet her eyes if he had a chance. Was he an animal, if music moved him so much? It seemed to him that someone was showing him the way to the unknown food. He had wanted this food for a long time. He decided to go to his sister and pull her skirt. In this way he would show her that she could come to his room with her violin. Nobody here liked her playing as much as he did. He never wanted to let her out of his room, at least not while he was alive. For once, his horrible look would be useful to him. He wanted to be at all the doors of his room at once, and hiss and spit at the attackers. But his sister should not be forced to stay with him. She should stay because she wanted to. She would sit next to him on the couch and bend her ear down to him. Then he would tell her about his plan. For a long time he had wanted to send her to the **conservatory**. He had wanted to tell everyone about it last Christmas, but then this bad luck came. (Was Christmas really over already?) And he would not let anybody change his mind. When his sister heard this, she would be so moved that she would cry. Gregor would climb up to her shoulder and kiss her neck. Since she had started working in the shop, she wore no **necklace** and no **collar**, and her neck was free.

"Mr Samsa!" the middle one of **the three lodgers** shouted to Gregor's father. He did not waste any more words. He pointed his finger at Gregor, who was slowly moving forward. The violin went quiet. The middle lodger smiled at his two friends and shook his head. Then he looked at Gregor again.

Gregor's father seemed to think it was more important to calm the lodgers first. He wanted to drive Gregor out after that. But the lodgers were not angry at all. They seemed to think Gregor was more interesting than the music. The father ran to them with his arms wide open. He tried to push them back into their room. At the same time, he tried to hide Gregor from their eyes with his body.

Now the lodgers did become a little angry. It was not clear why. Maybe they were angry at the father's behaviour. Maybe they were angry because they slowly understood something new. All this time they had had a neighbour like Gregor in the next room, and they had not known it. They asked the father for an explanation. They raised their arms, like he did, and pulled their beards nervously. Very slowly, they moved back towards their room.

Meanwhile, Gregor's sister was getting over her shock. When her playing stopped so suddenly, she had felt lost and without hope. For a while her hands dropped, and the violin and the bow hung in them without strength. She kept looking at the music, as if she was still playing. Then she pulled herself together. She put the violin on her mother's knees. Her mother was still sitting there and fighting for every breath. Then Grete ran into the lodgers' room. Her father was pushing the lodgers towards it, and they were now going faster.
Grete's hands were quick and sure. The pillows and blankets on the beds flew up and fell back in order. She had finished the beds and slipped out of the room before the lodgers reached it.

Gregor's father seemed to forget everything else. He forgot that he must be polite to the people who paid him rent. He pushed them and pushed them. At the door of the room, the middle lodger shouted like thunder and **stamped** his foot. The father stopped.

"I say this now," said the lodger. He raised his hand and looked at Gregor's mother and sister, because he wanted them to listen too. "Life in this flat and in this family is disgusting." Here he looked quickly but firmly at the floor. "So I give **notice** on my room now. Of course, I will not pay anything for the days I have lived here. In fact, I will think about asking you for money, because you have done me harm. Believe me, it would be very easy to give reasons for that."

He stopped talking and looked straight ahead. He seemed to be waiting for something. And his two friends did say something: "We give notice too." Then he took the door handle and closed the door with a bang.

Gregor's father walked back to his chair on weak, unsteady legs, feeling for it with his hands, and fell into it. It looked as if he wanted to sleep, as he did every evening. But his head kept falling forward without control, so it was clear that he was not sleeping at all.

All this time, Gregor lay still, in the place where the lodgers had first seen him. His plan had failed, and he was very sad. Maybe he was also weak because he was so hungry. He could not move. He was sure that everybody would turn against him in a moment, and he waited. Then the violin fell from his mother's shaking fingers and hit the floor with a loud noise. But even that did not frighten him.

"Father, Mother," said his sister, and she hit the table with her hand, "we cannot go on like this. Maybe you can't see it, but I can. I don't want to call this **monster** my brother. I can only say this: we must get rid of it. We have done everything a person can do. We looked after it, and we were patient. I think nobody can say that we did anything wrong."

"She is completely right," said Gregor's father quietly, to himself. His mother still could not breathe well. She began to cough, a dull cough. She held her hand out in front of her, and her eyes looked wild.

Gregor's sister ran to their mother and put a hand on her head. Her words seemed to give Gregor's father clearer thoughts. He sat up straight. He played with his uniform cap, which lay between the plates the lodgers had left after their meal. Sometimes he looked down at Gregor, who lay there without moving.

"We must get rid of it," said Gregor's sister. Now she spoke only to her father, because her mother was coughing too much to listen. "It will kill both of you. I can see it coming. We all have to work so hard. Then we come home and we are **tortured** like this. We can't bear it. I can't bear it any more." And she started to cry so much that her tears fell on her mother's face. Her mother wiped them away with her hand, without thinking, like a machine.
"My child," said her father kindly. He understood her well. "What can we do?"
His sister only lifted her shoulders. She was crying and she felt helpless. A moment before, she had been so sure. Now that feeling was gone.
"If he could only understand us," said her father. It was almost a question. Through her tears, his sister shook her hand hard, to say that this was impossible.

"If he could only understand us," her father said again. He closed his eyes, because he agreed with his daughter: it was quite impossible. "Then maybe we could make some kind of agreement with him. But as it is..."

"It must go!" shouted his sister. "That is the only way, Father. You must stop thinking that this is Gregor. We have believed it for too long, and it has only hurt us. How can this be Gregor? If it was Gregor, he would have understood a long time ago that people cannot live with an animal like this. He would have gone away by himself. Then we would not have a brother any more. But we could continue to live, and we could remember him with respect. But this animal follows us and hurts us. It has driven out our lodgers. It clearly wants the whole flat for itself, and it wants us to sleep in the street. Look, Father, just look!" she suddenly screamed. "He is starting again!"

She was so afraid, and Gregor could not understand why. She even left her mother. She jumped up from her chair, as if she would rather give up her own mother than stay near Gregor. She ran behind her father. He became nervous only because she was nervous. He stood up and half lifted his arms in front of Gregor's sister, as if he wanted to protect her.

But Gregor had not wanted to frighten anybody, and least of all his sister. He had only started to turn round, because he wanted to go back to his room. Of course, it did look frightening. He was in pain, and turning was very hard for him. He helped himself with his head: he lifted it again and again and hit it against the floor. Now he stopped and looked round. They seemed to understand that he meant well, and they had been afraid for only a moment. Now they all looked at him, sad and silent. His mother lay in her chair. Her legs were stretched out and pressed together, and her eyes were almost closed because she was so tired. His sister sat next to his father with her arms around his neck.

"Maybe now they will let me turn round," thought Gregor, and he went back to work. He could not stop breathing loudly because of the effort, and sometimes he had to stop and rest. Nobody was pushing him now. He could do everything in his own time. When he finally finished turning, he started to crawl straight ahead. He was surprised how far away his room was. A little while before, he had come all this way, and he had hardly noticed it. And he was so weak! He could not understand how he had done it.

He thought only about crawling as fast as he could. He hardly noticed that his family did not say a word and did not cry out. Nothing disturbed him. He did not turn his head until he reached the door. He did not turn it completely, because his neck was becoming **stiff**. But he could see that nothing behind him was different. Only his sister was now standing. His last look was at his mother, and she was now fast asleep.

Gregor was hardly inside his room when somebody quickly pushed the door shut, and locked it with the **bolt** and the key. The sudden noise behind him frightened him so much that his little legs gave way under him. It was his sister who had been in such a hurry. She was already standing there, waiting. Then she jumped forward lightly. Gregor did not hear her coming at all. She turned the key in the lock and said loudly to her parents, "At last!"

"And now?" Gregor asked himself, and he looked round in the dark. Soon he found that he could not move at all. He was not surprised. It seemed stranger to him that until now he had been able to move on those thin little legs. He felt quite comfortable. It was true that his whole body hurt. But the pain seemed to become weaker and weaker, and in the end it would go away completely. He could hardly feel the **rotten** apple in his back now. The red, painful place around it was covered with white dust, and he could hardly feel that either.

He thought about his family with love and deep feeling. He felt that he must go away. Maybe he felt it even more strongly than his sister did. He stayed in this empty and peaceful state of thinking until the clock tower struck three in the morning. He saw that it was slowly becoming light outside the window too. Then, by itself, his head sank down completely. And his last breath came out weakly through his nose.

Early in the morning **the cleaning woman** came. The family had often asked her not to bang the doors. But she was strong and always in a hurry, so she banged them anyway. When she came, everybody in the flat knew it, and after that nobody could sleep in peace. As usual, she looked into Gregor's room for a moment. At first she saw nothing special. She thought he was lying so still on purpose, because he wanted people to feel sorry for him. She believed he could understand everything.

She had a long broom in her hand, so she tried to **tickle** Gregor with it from the door. That did not work. Then she wanted to annoy him, and she pushed him a little. She found that she could push him across the floor, and he did not fight back at all. That was when she started to pay attention. Soon she understood what had really happened. Her eyes opened wide and she whistled to herself. But she did not waste time. She pulled open the doors of the bedroom and shouted loudly into the dark: "Come and look at this! It's dead! It's lying there, completely dead!"

Mr and Mrs Samsa sat up in their marriage bed. The cleaning woman gave them a shock. They needed some time to get over it. Only then could they understand what she said. But then each of them hurried out of bed from their own side. Mr Samsa put the blanket over his shoulders. Mrs Samsa came out in only her nightdress. And so they went into Gregor's room.

On the way, they opened the door of the living room. Grete had slept there since the lodgers moved in. She was fully dressed, as if she had not slept at all that night. Her pale face seemed to say the same. "Dead?" asked Mrs Samsa, and she looked at the cleaning woman with a question in her eyes. She could have checked it herself, and she could have known it even without checking. "That's what I said," answered the cleaning woman. To show it, she pushed Gregor's body with the broom again, and it slid sideways across the floor. Mrs Samsa moved as if she wanted to stop the broom, but she did not finish the movement.

"Well," said Mr Samsa, "let's thank God for that." He made the sign of the cross, and the three women did the same. Grete did not take her eyes off the dead body. She said, "Look how thin he was. He did not eat anything for such a long time. The food came out again, just the same as it went in." Gregor's body was really dry and flat. They had not seen this before. But now his little legs did not lift him up, and he did nothing to make them look away.

"Grete, come in here with us for a little while," said Mrs Samsa with a sad smile. Grete followed her parents into their bedroom, but she looked back at the body. The cleaning woman closed the door and opened the window wide. It was still early in the morning, but the fresh air was already a little warm. It was the end of March, after all.

The three lodgers came out of their room. They looked round in surprise and wanted their breakfast, but everybody had forgotten about it. "Where is our breakfast?" the middle lodger asked the cleaning woman angrily. She did not answer. She put her finger on her lips. Quickly and without a sound, she made a sign to the men to come into Gregor's room. They did, and stood round Gregor's dead body. Their hands were in the pockets of their old, worn coats. By now it was quite light in the room.

Then the door of the bedroom opened, and Mr Samsa came out in his uniform. His wife held one of his arms and his daughter held the other. All of them had cried a little before they came out. Now and then Grete pressed her face against her father's arm.

"Leave my home. Now!" said Mr Samsa, and he pointed at the door. He did not let go of the women. "What do you mean?" asked the middle lodger. He was a little confused, and he smiled in a sweet way. The other two kept their hands behind their backs and rubbed them together all the time. They were happy, because they expected a loud quarrel, and they were sure it would end well for them. "I mean exactly what I said," answered Mr Samsa. With the two women on his arms, he walked straight towards the lodger.

At first the man stood still and looked at the floor. It was as if his thoughts were moving to new places in his head. "All right, we will go," he said. Then he looked up at Mr Samsa. It seemed that he suddenly felt very small, and he wanted Mr Samsa to say yes to his decision once more. Mr Samsa only opened his eyes wide and quickly nodded to him a few times. Then the man really did walk into the hall with long steps, without waiting. His two friends were not rubbing their hands any more. They had stopped some time before and had listened to everything. Now they jumped after their friend. They seemed suddenly afraid that Mr Samsa could get into the hall before them and cut them off from their leader.

In the hall, all three took their hats from the stand and their sticks from the holder. They bowed without a word and left the flat. Mr Samsa and the two women followed them out to the **landing**. But they had no reason to think that the men would do anything bad. They leaned over the rail and watched the three lodgers going down the many steps, slowly but without stopping. At every floor they turned the corner and disappeared, and after a moment they came into view again. The further down they went, the less the Samsa family was interested in them. Then a boy from the meat shop came up the stairs. He carried a **tray** on his head and held himself very proudly. He passed the lodgers, and soon he was nearer to the family than the lodgers were. Then Mr Samsa and the women left the landing and went back into the flat, as if they felt relieved.

They decided to spend that day resting and walking. They worked hard, so they deserved a break, and they really needed one. So they sat down at the table and wrote three letters to say sorry for not coming to work. Mr Samsa wrote to his boss. Mrs Samsa wrote to the person she worked for. Grete wrote to her boss at the shop.

While they were writing, the cleaning woman came in. She said she was going now, because she had finished her work for the morning. At first the three of them only nodded and did not look up from their letters. But she did not go away, and then they looked up, annoyed. "Well?" asked Mr Samsa. The cleaning woman stood in the doorway and smiled. It looked as if she had wonderful news. But she would tell it only if somebody asked her clearly. The small **ostrich feather** on her hat stood almost straight up. This feather had annoyed Mr Samsa all the time she had worked for them. Now it moved gently in every direction.

"What do you want?" asked Mrs Samsa. The cleaning woman respected her most. "Yes," she answered. She laughed in a friendly way, so she could not speak for a moment. "Well, about that thing in there. You don't have to worry about how to get rid of it. It's all done." Mrs Samsa and Grete bent over their letters, as if they wanted to go on writing. Mr Samsa saw that the cleaning woman wanted to tell them everything. He put out his hand and made it clear that she must not. So she could not tell them all about it, and she suddenly remembered that she was in a great hurry. She was clearly hurt and angry. "Goodbye, everybody," she called, turned round fast, and left. She banged the door terribly behind her.

"Tonight she will lose her job," said Mr Samsa. But his wife and daughter did not answer. It seemed that the cleaning woman had destroyed the peace they had found only a short time before. They got up and went to the window. They stood there with their arms round each other. Mr Samsa turned round in his chair and watched them for a while. Then he called to them: "Come here. Let's forget all the old things, shall we? Come and give me a little attention." The two women came at once. They hurried to him, kissed him and hugged him. Then they quickly finished their letters.

After that, the three of them left the flat together. It was the first time in many months. They took the **tram** to the open country outside the town. The tram was full of warm sunshine, and they were the only people in it. They leaned back comfortably in their seats and talked about their future. When they looked at it more closely, it was not bad at all. Until then they had never asked each other about their work. But now they saw that all three jobs were very good, and they could become even better in the future.

The biggest improvement for now would be easy: they could move to another flat. They needed one that was smaller and cheaper than this one. Gregor had chosen this flat. The new flat should be in a better place and, most of all, more practical. All this time Grete was becoming livelier. In the last few months the family had had so many worries, and her cheeks had become pale. But while they talked, Mr and Mrs Samsa both saw something, almost at the same moment. Their daughter was growing into a beautiful young woman with a strong, healthy body. They became quieter. Just by looking at each other, and almost without knowing it, they agreed. Soon it would be time to find a good husband for her.
And when they arrived, Grete was the first to stand up. She stretched her young body. It was like a sign that their new dreams and good plans were right.

questions.q: True or false: After the apple hit him, Gregor could move easily again.
questions.answer: False. He moved very slowly and with difficulty.

questions.q: True or false: The family sent the maid away because they had little money.
questions.answer: True. They had less and less money.

questions.q: True or false: The three lodgers liked Grete's violin music very much.
questions.answer: False. They were bored and only listened to be polite.

questions.q: Why did Grete get angry when her mother cleaned Gregor's room?
questions.answer: Because only she wanted to clean his room.

questions.q: Why did the three lodgers say they wanted to leave?
questions.answer: Because the flat and the family were dirty and horrible, and they saw Gregor.

questions.q: What did Grete say about Gregor to her parents?
questions.answer: She said it was not Gregor and they must get rid of it.

questions.q: What did the family do after Gregor died?
questions.answer: They wrote letters, then took the tram to the country and talked about the future.
